summary:
SPHEREx TimeLens is an astronomical analysis platform for exploring potential transient and variable sources in multi-epoch infrared observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. It brings archive access, image processing and AI-assisted candidate analysis into one workflow.

The platform uses IRSA SIA2 queries and processes FITS observations with Python, Astropy and a FastAPI backend. Its pipeline includes World Coordinate System (WCS) alignment, image differencing, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) mapping and uncertainty-aware candidate detection. An Isolation Forest model helps rank possible changes while the system accounts for noise and instrumental artefacts.

Users can compare observations across epochs, review scientifically qualified candidates, track alerts, inspect light curves and export results in JSON, CSV and VOEvent formats. A separate synthetic demo mode supports exploration when the live archive is unavailable, without mixing simulated data with real observations.

The project aims to make infrared time-domain analysis more accessible, traceable and scientifically cautious.
details:
Our project, **SPHEREx TimeLens**, is a software platform developed to study changes in astronomical objects using infrared observations collected at different points in time by NASA's SPHEREx mission.

The platform is designed to retrieve observations through the IRSA SIA2 archive interface and process FITS images for multi-epoch analysis. It uses image alignment based on World Coordinate System (WCS), image differencing and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) mapping to identify regions that may have changed between observations. An Isolation Forest machine-learning model assists in identifying and ranking potential candidates for further examination. Users can compare observations, inspect candidate sources, view light curves, track alerts and export analysis results.

The main benefit is bringing several stages of astronomical data analysis into one application instead of requiring users to work with separate tools and manually connect their results. This can make the investigation process more organised and accessible, particularly when examining large sets of observations.

We developed the project using Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, React, TypeScript and Vite. It is entirely software-based; no dedicated hardware is required. We also included a separate synthetic demo mode so the application can be explored when the live archive is unavailable.

What makes TimeLens distinctive is its combination of traditional image-processing techniques and machine learning within a single multi-epoch workflow. We paid particular attention to image registration, noise, instrumental artefacts, measurement uncertainty and the risk of false detections. The system treats detected changes as potential candidates, not confirmed astronomical discoveries.

Our aim is to provide a practical tool that helps researchers explore time-dependent infrared observations and investigate potentially interesting astronomical events with greater clarity and traceability.
